transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lena (Vesper Head of ML), Tom (Vesper Platform Eng), Priya (Vesper SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be incomplete):
- Align on TTFT vs TPOT acceptance criteria for pilot; agree sampling plan and traffic shaping; collect traffic traces and prompt corpus; schedule benchmark run; discuss security constraints (SOC2, KMS, VPC).
- Major tradeoffs: p95 vs p99 targets, batching/kv-cache impact on TPOT, canary routing and fallback models.

Topics: SLO hypothesis, sampling & measurement plan, pilot timeline, security requirements, success criteria and rollout triggers.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we have Lena, Tom, Priya on the Vesper side; Ethan and I from Redwood. Quick agenda: align on SLO hypothesis (TTFT vs TPOT), define p95/p99 targets, agree sampling plan and next steps for the benchmark.

[00:23] Lena: Yep thanks. Main goals for us — must be predictable latency for customer-facing chat (low TTFT) but also need to bound per-token cost. We'll have compliance folks watching security posture.

[00:40] Ethan: Great. To be explicit, when I say TTFT I mean time to first token from request arrival at ingress; TPOT is per-token generation tail behavior — essentially total completion latency per response or cost-per-token implications.

[01:12] Tom: Quick Q, do you typically measure TTFT at the LB or at the model worker? We want numbers that reflect user perceived latency, so LB-side seems right.

[01:30] Ethan: Good call. For this pilot let's measure TTFT at the API ingress (edge) and correlate with model worker metrics. We'll capture both so we can separate network/edge vs worker time.

[02:05] Priya: Also, we need p95 and p99. For user-facing chat, p95 is our main SLA, p99 is more for alerting. Target ranges?

[02:22] Maya: Based on similar pilots, initial hypothesis: TTFT p95 <= 150ms for short prompts (<= 64 tokens), p99 <= 350ms. For TPOT, p95 per-token generation latency should be such that 95% of completions finish within X ms — we usually express TPOT as average per-token and tail of completion for typical 64-128 token responses. But we want your input.

[03:00] Lena: 150ms p95 sounds ambitious but acceptable if you can show it on hosted. Our users are sensitive; for longer documents we accept higher TTFT but want consistent p99 behavior.

[03:24] Ethan: Let's set concrete matrices. Proposal: sample traffic split by prompt size buckets: short (<=64), medium (65-256), long (>256). For short: TTFT p95 150ms, p99 350ms. For medium: TTFT p95 250ms, p99 600ms. Long: p95 600ms, p99 1500ms. For TPOT we'll set per-token time budgets and total completion budgets: e.g., average token generation < 10ms, completion p95 for 64-token response < 700ms.

[04:12] Tom: Can you show how batching affects TTFT? Our traffic is spiky; batching could improve cost but increase TTFT.

[04:31] Ethan: Absolutely. Measurement plan includes toggling batch sizes and prefix caching. We'll run three modes in the benchmark: no batching (single request), small batching (batch size 4-8), and aggressive batching (16-32) to show tradeoffs. We'll capture TTFT at edge and per-worker queuing.

[05:05] Priya: We also use a KV cache for repeated prompts; can you measure cache hit vs miss performance?

[05:19] Ethan: Yes — we'll include a prefix/KV cache hit rate sweep in the run. For cache-hit traces we'll replay sequences with repeated contexts to estimate savings on TPOT and token cost.

[05:40] Lena: On sampling: we can give you 7 days of anonymized request traces (timestamps, prompt lengths, client region, and 1% sample of prompt text). Is that enough?

[05:55] Maya: That's perfect. Ideal format is CSV with request_ts, prompt_len, response_len_est, success_flag, and optionally a small prompt sample. That will let us synthesize realistic traffic profiles.

[06:18] Tom: Security note — we need data residency and KMS controls. For pilot we might do hosted but with dedicated VPC peering or Dedicated mode. What options?

[06:35] Maya: We can run the pilot on Redwood Dedicated or Private depending on your compliance. For the initial benchmark it's easiest to run on a Redwood Dedicated pool in your region; we'll provide SOC2 docs and options for customer-managed KMS for the Private path. I'll share the checklist.

[07:00] Priya: Please include audit log granularity — we need request-level logs and token usage with user identifiers masked.

[07:12] Ethan: We'll enable request-level tracing for the benchmark and sanitize PII. We'll also produce per-route latency breakdowns and cost token counts.

[07:45] Lena: What about load shaping — we want to test at concurrency 50, 200, and 800. Our peak is around 500 concurrent small-chat connections.

[08:00] Ethan: Noted. We'll run a load sweep: 50 -> 200 -> 500 -> 800 concurrency with steady-state windows (10 minutes each) and a short spike burst to see queueing effects. We'll capture p95/p99 at each point.

[08:25] Tom: For benchmarks, do you use synthetic prompts or replay our real prompts?

[08:35] Ethan: Both. Replay your trace for realism; supplement with synthetic worst-case prompts to stress attention/long-context behavior. We'll use your prompt corpus to build a sampler that preserves prompt length distribution and tokens per response.

[09:02] Maya: Acceptance criteria proposal: Pilot passes if: 1) For short-bucket at your projected peak concurrency (500), TTFT p95 <= 200ms and p99 <= 400ms; 2) TPOT cost per 1k tokens within 15% of expected budget; 3) No unrecoverable errors under 800 concurrency and fallback routing works. If these are met we move to a month-long canary.

[09:38] Lena: That feels reasonable; the p95 guard is primary. We'll flag a separate threshold for tail-latency alerts.

[09:50] Priya: Also want a rollback plan — if p99 jumps during rollout we need automatic fallback to a higher-capacity model or reduced batching.

[10:04] Ethan: We support automatic fallback policies by weight — canary to full rollouts and instant fallback to a less-quantized but lower-latency variant. We'll document the policy for you.

[10:30] Tom: Will you measure cold-start behavior for KV cache misses? We care about session-first-turn latency.

[10:45] Ethan: Yes — we'll capture cold vs warmed cache TTFT. For cold we expect higher TTFT; we'll quantify it and propose mitigations (pre-warming, smart sticky routing).

[11:10] Lena: One nit: how do you compute TPOT for multi-turn chat where tokens are streamed? We need an apples-to-apples metric.

[11:24] Ethan: Good point. We'll define TPOT as: total server-side token generation time per response (sum of per-token generation intervals) and also report mean token generation time and completion latency. For streaming, we'll capture time to each token as well as time to final token.

[11:50] Maya: We'll include both: per-token average and completion p95. For sampling, we'll record event-level timestamps so you can reconstruct streaming behavior.

[12:10] Tom: Bench infrastructure — will you provide the benchmark harness and scripts so we can reproduce locally?

[12:20] Ethan: Yes. We'll push a benchmark repo with scripts, traffic generator, and a measurement dashboard. We're planning an initial 2-hour run so you can see the raw metrics and artifacts.

[12:40] Priya: SLA around uptime for dedicated pool during benchmark? We need guarantees for experiment reproducibility.

[12:50] Maya: We'll allocate reserved capacity for the window and include an incident contact. For the pilot we'll give a best-effort SLA for the benchmark period and a follow-up run if cloud variance affects results.

[13:15] Lena: Okay timeline recap — we want Redwood to draft SLO matrix and sampling plan by 10/28; we'll hand over traces and corpus by 10/29; preliminary script from Redwood by 10/27; schedule benchmark for week of 11/08. Does that align?

[13:35] Maya: Yes. I'll put those in the notes and update the next steps.

[13:48] Tom: One last ops question — for Dedicated mode, how does quantization interact with your fallback policies? If we quantize a model to save cost, what's the expected p99 delta?

[14:05] Ethan: It depends on model and quant level. Empirically, 8-bit quantization can increase variance — p99 may shift by ~10-20% depending on kernel selection and sequence length. We'll include a quantization matrix in the results and recommend hybrid strategy: quantize for non-critical routes and keep a warm unquantized fallback.

[14:40] Priya: Great. Any competitor concerns? We looked at Anthropic for some experiments; any notes on comparative latencies?

[14:54] Maya: We won't do a direct competitor bake-off in pilot but can share redwood-verified performance profiles for similar models so you can compare.

[15:10] Lena: Alright let's wrap. Thanks — the follow-ups are clear.

[15:20] Maya: Recap of next steps: Redwood sends SLO matrix & sampling plan (10/28), Ethan pushes measurement script (10/27), Vesper shares traces and corpus (10/29), book benchmark week of 11/08. We'll also send SOC2/KMS checklist and a proposed dedicated pool config.

[15:45] Tom: Sounds good.

[15:50] Meeting ends.
